beats.text: An exponential equation asks which input produces a target output. Six lies between the outputs four and eight, so the needed exponent lies between two and three. Graphing gives this estimate, while logarithms give an exact expression.

A logarithm names the exponent rather than approximating by trial and error. Taking natural logarithms of both sides and using the power rule gives x times natural log of two equals natural log of six, leading to the change-of-base formula.

Logarithm laws also depend on domains. Combining the sum into a product requires both original arguments to be positive, which means x is greater than one. Simplifying their product must not introduce negative inputs excluded by either original logarithm.

Equating the combined logarithm with natural log of four gives x squared minus one equals four. Algebra suggests positive or negative square root of five, but the original condition x greater than one keeps only the positive candidate.

practice.prompt: Solve 3ˣ=11 using logarithms; an exact expression is sufficient.
State the real domain before simplifying ln(x−2)+ln(x+2).
practice.answer: Both arguments must be positive, sox>2. The sum becomesln(x²−4) only on that original domain.

practice.prompt: Solve ln(x−2)+ln(x+2)=ln(5), checking candidates against the original domain.

takeaway: Logarithms invert positive-base exponentials; log laws retain every original argument restriction.
scope: Change of base, exponential solving, logarithm laws, and domain checks.
title: Advanced exponentials and logs
objective: Solve exponential and logarithmic models with valid bases and domains.
